input.question: Why do storage devices such as hard drives, flash drives, and memory cards never have as much free space as the packaging says?
input.ground_truth: The SD card manufacturer measures data using standard metric measurements (1 GB = 10^9 B), while your computer uses binary versions of the measurement (1 GB = 2^30 B) since computers count in binary. So the computer's gigabyte (often listed as GiB to avoid confusion) is about 7% larger than the normal definition of a GB. Your flash drive still holds 32 billion bytes, but your computer reports those 32 billion bytes as 29GB and some change.

Okay! Imagine you buy a big toy box, and on the box it says, "Holds 100 toys!" But when you try to put your toys inside, you find that you can only fit about 90 toys. Why?

Well, here’s why:  
The number on the box is like the biggest possible number of toys it *could* hold if everything was perfect. But in real life, some space is taken up by the toy box’s own little things—like the bottom, the sides, or even the way the toys have to be arranged so they don’t fall out. Also, sometimes the box has a label or a sticker that takes up a little space.

It’s the same with your storage devices, like a USB stick or a memory card. The number on the package is the biggest number they *could* hold if everything was perfect. But the device itself needs some space for its own “brain” and instructions, and sometimes a little space is used to help the computer talk to the device. So, you never get the full number—some space is always used up by the device itself!
